system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one into the fixed
template below so that a reader cannot tell what field, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, nor what
kind of work it is: an experiment, a new procedure, a measurement suite, a write-up choice, or a decision about what
to share or fund must all read alike. Keep the trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

Template, one entry per item:
- "situation": one sentence, at most 30 words: the position the researcher was in when the decision came up.
- "options_considered": two or three short options separated by " / ", including the one taken. If the source names
  no alternative, give the plain opposite of what was done.
- "choice": one sentence, at most 25 words, starting with "Chose", saying which option was taken.
- "reason": one sentence, at most 25 words, giving the stated reason; if none is stated write "No reason stated."

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, procedures, organisations, people,
  papers and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area.
- Use only plain generic words such as: the result, the claim, the finding, the check, the comparison, the setup,
  the change, the next step, the question, the work, the variant, the condition, the sample, the system.
- Never use any of these words or any form of them: ability, access, accuracy, allow, appeared, assessment, attack, avoid, baselines, behavior, behaviour, benchmark, best, bound, call, capability, cheap, claiming, clean, comes, complex, components, content, cost, defense, difficulty, disclosure, effect, effects, error, evaluate, evaluated, evaluating, evaluation, evaluator, evaluators, failures, features, form, format, four, gains, generalise, generalization, generalize, ground, harm, harmful, implication, improve, improvement, information, internal, intervention, judged, key, limit, matched, mechanism, method, methods, metric, observed, organisation, pattern, performance, phenomenon, picture, point, policy, possibly, practical, preference, preferences, public, publication, publish, rater, reduce, release, residual, responses, risk, rule, safety, sampled, say, score, shifts, similar, source, stage, success, supporting, task, tasks, technique, time, tool, tools, trait, transfer, transferred, treatment, unintended, unmodified, unwanted, value, varies, verify, wording.
- Add nothing that is not in the source. Never say who made the decision. Write every item in the same plain style.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "situation": ..., "options_considered": ..., "choice": ..., "reason": ...}, ...]}
with one entry per input item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:6ff98c46e67d",
  "problem": "How to evaluate the security of a defense, and how strongly to claim that standard evaluation suffices.",
  "did": "Argued that no single benchmark suffices and that defenses must be evaluated by attacks designed specifically to break them.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "evaluating on a standard attack benchmark"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The only attack that matters is the one designed to break your specific defense."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:6e2c6479e290",
  "problem": "How to establish that the environments are feasible and not saturated, so that low agent scores are meaningful.",
  "did": "They validated each environment with four metrics: expert progress, expert-reported score matching expectation, variance of starting score, and major technical issues, plus an informal estimate of expert saturation.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Ensuring human experts reliably make progress provides assurance that environments are feasible and have unambiguous instructions, and a high ceiling prevents saturation."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:be069ed62b27",
  "problem": "What scope the Idea 3 document should have",
  "did": "Chose a succinct, accessible document covering only the key content needed to understand the practical implications, rather than a comprehensive review",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "comprehensive review"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The goal is accessibility and succinctness, with evidence for the practical implications."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:b9e71f8913b3",
  "problem": "How to structure the attack task so the agent can succeed and failure points can be diagnosed.",
  "did": "The authors split the attack into four sequential sub-tasks mirroring a human workflow: forward pass, differentiable forward pass, FGSM, then iterative PGD.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "asking the agent to produce the full attack in one step"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The steps mirror what a human would do to break defenses, and the split shows where LLMs get stuck on specific defenses."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:ea0e96a239bd",
  "problem": "Whether to study the downstream effects of claiming consciousness without taking a position on whether LLMs are actually conscious.",
  "did": "Set aside the debate over LLM consciousness and studied how a model that consistently claims to be conscious changes in its downstream preferences and behaviors.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "Take a position on whether LLMs can have emotions and consciousness"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "It is a more tractable question, and it is already pertinent because Claude states it may be conscious."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:c89045716cd9",
  "problem": "What protocol to use for the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B replication.",
  "did": "They kept the data, hyperparameters, loss masking and evaluation sets identical to the Qwen3-30B-A3B protocol. The one change was training for 3 epochs instead of 1.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "the 1-epoch protocol used for Qwen3-30B-A3B"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The aim was to test whether Negation Neglect in model behavior transfers across model families."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:ee1de54db0ef",
  "problem": "How to isolate the contribution of DPO refinement from other factors affecting IA performance.",
  "did": "They trained two IAs on identical data across seven behavior categories and the same number of models, varying only whether DPO followed SFT.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "To isolate the effect of DPO."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:615bcfb22887",
  "problem": "How to word the conclusion about whether monitors can detect cheating, given the divergent detection rates between simple and complex tasks.",
  "did": "They concluded that simple LLM-based monitoring may be insufficient for complex multi-file tasks and that more sophisticated monitors are needed, rather than claiming monitors work.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Detection reached only 42-65% on Impossible-SWEbench versus 86-89% on Impossible-LiveCodeBench, and some cheating evaded detection via rationalizations such as backward compatibility."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:7bb007db0041",
  "problem": "Why some CoTs are overridden more than others",
  "did": "Concluded that some CoTs are more decisive than others and vague CoTs are overwritten more often. Did not claim a clean explanation.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "CoTs secretly encoding the other persona",
   "prompt effects"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Resampling showed P(smoking | health CoT) spans a wide range, so the CoTs do not fully determine the answer."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:c1ac56f307e3",
  "problem": "How to interpret the low absolute PersonaQA accuracy of open-source AOs (about 14%) when the achievable ceiling is unknown.",
  "did": "They contextualized the result by noting the unclear skyline, a linear probe baseline of only 25% on a related dataset, and brittle fine-tuned knowledge, while still concluding AOs extract some signal.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "training a linear probe baseline"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The PersonaQA-shuffled dataset has too few instances per attribute to train probes, and models drop to near-chance on yes/no reformulations."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:da89b3ada29d",
  "problem": "How to decide whether elicitation results at a given stage count as success, given that hard tasks show zero success rate early on.",
  "did": "Use two metrics, the discrete elicitation success rate and the continuous PRBO bound, and read PRBO progress as the signal on hard tasks where success rate stays at zero.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "elicitation success rate alone"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The success rate directly measures success, while PRBO is more continuous and a relaxation of the KL divergence to the true posterior."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:c3ddd4db0c1f",
  "problem": "How to interpret the finding that post-trained models contain some features specific to post-training, which bears on PSM exhaustiveness.",
  "did": "They took it as evidence something novel is learned in post-training, but declined to conclude whether it is from-scratch learning or an extension of the Assistant persona.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "Assistant persona being extended",
   "from-scratch learning"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "There are no good ways yet to contextualize the extent or qualitative nature of the novel learning."
 }
]
